newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire's Premier resigns as rebels advance.
newsitem.headline: Zaire's Premier resigns as rebels advance.

text.p: Zaire's Kengo wa Dondo, who resigned as prime minister on Monday in the face of a five-month rebel advance in the country's east, had many political enemies who made it difficult for him to hang on to his post.

Kengo, the compromise choice in 1994 for prime minister in a bitterly divided field, fell out of favour as the rebels took more territory. The transitional parliament voted to oust him from office last week in a move Kengo declared unconstitutional.

Political analysts said Kengo's decision to quit was inevitable after President Mobutu Sese Seko, who returned from cancer treatment in Europe last week, effectively backed parliament's position on Monday, saying he "took note" of the anti-Kengo vote.
Mobutu in December issued a decree naming Kengo as the head of a new crisis cabinet to guide the war effort to retake land from ethnic Tutsi-led rebels in eastern Zaire.

But the ill-disciplined Zairean army was unable to stem the rebel successes and Kengo was an easy target for opposition politicians, who among other things accused him of not being a true Zairean because of his mixed parentage.
Born in 1934, Kengo's father was a Polish Jew naturalised as a Belgian. His mother is said to have been half Tutsi and half Ngbandi, the tribe of Mobutu's Equateur region Kengo grew up in.

Recently, Kengo's many enemies exploited his part-Tutsi origins to promote popular hatred of the premier. They argued he was not Zairean and so unqualified to lead the country in the war against ethnic Tutsi-led rebels said by Kinshasa to be backed by Tutsi-led armies in neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi.

Kengo served under Mobutu on numerous occasions in Zaire's turbulent post-independence history. He was prime minister in 1982-86 and again from 1988 to 1990, before the transition from one-party rule.

He came back to the top of the government in 1994 when he was elected by a newly installed majority in the transitional parliament. He was said at the time to have been a consensus candidate who, unlike Mobutu's radical opponent Etienne Tshisekedi, could work with Zaire's all-powerful ruler.

His post was bitterly contested by Tshisekedi, who since being shunted aside in favour of a Mobutu appointee in 1993 has claimed to be the only legitimate prime minister elected by a sovereign national conference.

Under Zaire's transitional constitution, opposition parties can designate the prime minister. Following Kengo's resignation they were due to meet and Tshisekedi was one of the leading candidates, political sources said.

Kengo also had many enemies in the president's entourage, especially among those who profited from the country's diamond trade. They were financially damaged in 1994 when Kengo expelled members of the Lebanese community who he accused of oiling the motor of the illicit trade.
Kengo, who had a reputation as a sound financial manager despite failing to halt Zaire's disasterous economic decline during his previous terms as premier, himself is reputed to have enormous wealth.
Personal friends, however, skirt over his long career as a member of Mobutu's one-party regime and say that he is a rigorous man of the law true to his education and early training as a lawyer.
"He is the prototype of a jurist, rigorous and obedient to the text," said one close ally, who added that he played tennis almost every morning.
Married with children, Kengo is also a practicising Roman Catholic and has been reported to read the Bible while travelling by plane.
